summary: Describes the multicast VPN solution designed and deployed by Cisco Systems for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs. It largely overlaps with the IETF framework standardized later and is documented because it was deployed before. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Before an official way existed, one company built its own method for sending one-to-many traffic through private networks. This writes it down for the record.

subtitle: Cisco's method for sending multicast through BGP/MPLS IP VPNs.

tldr.problem: BGP/MPLS IP VPNs support unicast traffic but not multicast. Extending multicast support while keeping routing state bounded and transparent to customers required new protocols and procedures.
tldr.mechanism: Cisco's solution uses multicast routing instances (PIM C-instances) within each VPN, connected through multicast tunnels (MDTs) in the provider network. It also defines a default MDT for control traffic and data MDTs for high-traffic groups, plus BGP extensions (MDT-SAFI) to auto-discover PE routers in the same domain.
tldr.outcome: The IETF later standardized a more generalized MVPN framework that makes different choices (e.g., using MPLS P2MP LSPs instead of just multicast trees). This document is historic and preserved as a reference for deployed Cisco implementations.

today: RFC 6037 is Historic. The IETF later standardized a more generalized multicast VPN framework that replaces much of this work with MPLS P2MP and MP2MP Label Switched Paths in addition to multicast tree support. Cisco's solution is documented here for historical reference and to describe deployed implementations that predate the standards.

sections.title: Multicast in Private Networks
sections.content:
BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, defined in RFC 4364, allow enterprises to create private networks that overlay a service provider's backbone. These VPNs support unicast traffic: a packet destined to one address is routed across the backbone following the shortest path, and the provider backbone routers maintain no VPN-specific state.

However, RFC 4364 provides no way for IP multicast (one-to-many traffic) to travel between VPN sites. This RFC extends the framework to support multicast while maintaining the key scalability property: the provider backbone routers maintain state proportional only to the number of VPNs, not to the number of multicast groups or transmitters.

The solution assumes Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) running within each VPN, and native IPv4 multicast forwarding in the provider network. The trade-off for scalability is that multicast routing is less optimal: a PE router may receive multicast packets for groups with no local receivers and must discard them.
sections.plainLanguage: When you have a private network (VPN) run by a service provider, you want to send one message to many people at once (like a video stream). This is how Cisco did it.

sections.title: VPN Multicast Infrastructure
sections.content:
The solution introduces multicast VRFs: each VPN routing and forwarding table now includes multicast routing entries, not just unicast. Within each VRF, a PE router runs its own instance of PIM-SM, called a PIM C-instance (C for "customer VPN"). Each C-instance maintains adjacencies with PIM-capable CE (customer edge) routers associated with that VRF.

The provider backbone runs a separate, provider-wide instance of PIM-SM called the PIM P-instance (P for "provider"). PE and P routers run the P-instance; P routers do not run C-instances at all.

A Multicast Domain is a set of VRFs associated with interfaces that can send multicast traffic to each other. Each multicast domain is configured with a Default MDT group address, an IPv4 multicast address used to build the default multicast distribution tree through the provider backbone. This Default MDT connects all PE routers in the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside each customer's VPN, there is a separate multicast system. The provider network has its own multicast system. A tunnel connects them.

sections.title: Multicast Tunnels and Data Flow
sections.content:
A Multicast Tunnel (MT) connects PE routers in the same multicast domain. From a VPN-specific PIM instance's perspective, the MT appears as a single multi-access interface, as if all PEs were connected to an Ethernet switch. In the provider network, an MT is realized as a Default MDT combined with zero or more Data MDTs.

When a multicast packet arrives from a customer (CE) router at an ingress PE, the PE encapsulates the packet in GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) with the destination address set to the Default MDT group address, and sends it into the provider network. All egress PEs (those with receivers in the same multicast domain) receive and decapsulate the packet.

To ensure the MT is treated as a multi-access interface, PIM control packets (Hellos, Join/Prune, Assert) are also encapsulated and sent over the Default MDT. This allows PE routers to run PIM adjacency and designated forwarder election over the logical interface, just as if they were on a LAN.

When a PE needs to determine the reverse-path-forwarding neighbor for a customer multicast address, it uses a Connector Attribute distributed via BGP. This attribute specifies the source IP address that the upstream PE will use for encapsulated multicast packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The PE routers act as if they are all on the same network, even though they are separated by the provider's backbone. Multicast packets are wrapped in a provider-network header and sent across.

sections.title: Auto-Discovery and Inter-AS Support
sections.content:
To set up a Default MDT, PE routers need to know which other PEs belong to the same multicast domain. RFC 6037 defines MDT-SAFI, a new BGP address family (SAFI 66) for auto-discovery. A PE advertises an MDT-SAFI route containing its own IPv4 address, a Route Distinguisher (RD) for the multicast domain, and the multicast group address to use as the Default MDT.

MDT-SAFI routes are distributed using standard BGP route-target-based filtering. Each PE learns the addresses of all other PEs in its multicast domain, and the group address is used to identify which multicast domain each PE belongs to.

For inter-AS (multi-provider) multicast domains, RFC 6037 defines the MVPN Join Attribute, a PIM extension that allows a PE to tell PIM to construct trees through a specific BGP next-hop (the AS border router) rather than directly to the source. This enables the inter-AS part of the multicast tree to follow a path optimized for multicast, rather than merely following the unicast topology.
sections.plainLanguage: The PE routers use BGP to announce "I am part of multicast domain X and will listen on group address Y." They learn which other PEs are in the same domain and which group to use.

sections.title: Data MDT Optimization
sections.content:
Using only a default MDT means all multicast traffic for a VPN domain is flooded to all PE routers, even those without receivers for that group. For high-traffic groups with few receivers, this wastes backbone bandwidth and PE resources.

RFC 6037 therefore defines Data MDTs. When traffic to a particular multicast group exceeds a configured threshold, the ingress PE announces an MDT Join TLV—a signaling message containing the source and group addresses, plus a new multicast group address to use for that flow. Egress PEs with actual receivers for that group join the Data MDT group, creating an optimal distribution tree in the provider network. The ingress PE then switches to encapsulating that flow to the Data MDT group instead.

Data MDT signaling uses UDP messages sent over the Default MDT. The PE periodically re-announces the MDT Join TLV at a configured interval; if an egress PE does not receive it for longer than a timeout (default 3 minutes), the PE leaves the Data MDT group and stops receiving that flow.

RFC 6037 recommends using Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) for Data MDTs, as it simplifies the assignment of group addresses and scales better as the number of flows increases.
sections.plainLanguage: When one group becomes very popular, the network is smart enough to create a special tunnel just for that group, so PE routers with no interest do not have to receive it.
